question_the_bucket_answers: Which indexing structure should back this array workload?
why_exclusive: Exactly one is correct once two facts are fixed: what mutates (nothing / one cell / whole spans) and what algebra the aggregate has (invertible, idempotent, or neither). Choosing prefix sums when updates exist is wrong; paying for lazy propagation on a frozen array is wrong. The members differ by ONE condition each, not by subject. Deliberately EXCLUDES complexity:24 ('segment trees need the combining operation to be associative') and complexity:26 (sparse tables degrade on sums), which share the area and category but are CONSTRAINTS that hold alongside a member rather than competing with it -- that is the trap this whole file exists to avoid.

members.recipe: Static array, many range-sum queries: prefix sums, O(n) build then O(1) per query. In 2D the same idea gives O(NM) build with four lookups per submatrix query.
members.trigger_condition: Are there many range-sum queries with no updates?

members.recipe: Point updates interleaved with range sums: Fenwick tree, O(log N) update, O(log N) query, O(N) space. Easier to code than a segment tree, especially multidimensional.
members.trigger_condition: Are there range-sum queries on a mutating array?

members.recipe: Range updates plus range queries: segment tree with lazy propagation, O(log n) each. The update must be composable so deferred updates combine, and must apply uniformly to a whole segment.
members.trigger_condition: Must a single update modify an entire range?

members.recipe: Immutable array, range min/max/gcd: sparse table, O(N log N) build then O(1) per query. O(1) needs an idempotent operation where double-counting an overlap is harmless.
members.trigger_condition: Is the array immutable with idempotent range aggregates?

members.recipe: Aggregate has no clean segment-tree merge but blocks can be summarised: sqrt decomposition into sqrt(n) blocks, O(n) preprocess, O(sqrt(n)) per query. Simpler to write than a lazy segment tree.
members.trigger_condition: Is the aggregate awkward to merge in a segment tree?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which distance algorithm does this graph admit?
why_exclusive: The members are separated by single properties of the input -- sign of the weights, how many distinct weights exist, one source versus every pair. Each property makes exactly one member correct and at least one other member outright invalid (Dijkstra is wrong, not merely slow, with a negative edge). Not a topical split: all four are single-source-or-all-pairs distance over a weighted graph.

members.recipe: Non-negative weights on a sparse graph: Dijkstra with a priority queue, O(m log n). On a dense graph where m approaches n^2 the plain array version at O(n^2 + m) is preferable.
members.trigger_condition: Are all edge weights non-negative?

members.recipe: Every edge weight is 0 or 1: skip the heap entirely. 0-1 BFS with a deque, pushing weight-0 edges to the front and weight-1 to the back, runs in O(E).
members.trigger_condition: Is every edge weight in the set {0,1}?

members.recipe: Any negative edge weight present: Dijkstra is invalid. Bellman-Ford runs n-1 relaxation phases in O(nm), and one extra phase that still relaxes proves a negative cycle exists.
members.trigger_condition: Can any edge weight be negative?

members.recipe: All-pairs distances with n at most a few hundred: Floyd-Warshall, O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space. Tolerates negative edges; a negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle.
members.trigger_condition: Do you need distances between every pair of vertices?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which string technique does this matching workload need?
why_exclusive: One text and one needle, one text and tens of thousands of needles, and arbitrary-substring equality are three different questions about the same subject, and the correct answer flips entirely on how many patterns there are and whether the comparison endpoints are known in advance.

members.recipe: One pattern in one text: prefix function on pattern + separator + text gives all occurrences in O(n+m) with O(n) space. Also yields the smallest period as n minus the last prefix value.
members.trigger_condition: Are you searching for a single fixed pattern?

members.recipe: Many patterns against one text: Aho-Corasick builds a trie with suffix links in O(m*k) over total pattern length, then scans in O(len + ans). Running KMP per pattern would be O(n*m).
members.trigger_condition: Are you matching a dictionary of patterns at once?

members.recipe: Repeated equality tests between arbitrary substrings: polynomial prefix hashes, O(n) precompute then O(1) per comparison, versus O(min(n1,n2)) for direct comparison.
members.trigger_condition: Do you compare arbitrary substring pairs many times?

question_the_bucket_answers: The constraints are fixed -- what running time is the intended solution?
why_exclusive: Every member is the same sentence about the same subject with a different number in it. Nothing topical separates them at all; only the stated bound does. This is the most extreme contrastive bucket in the file and the cleanest test of whether a mechanism reads the CONDITION rather than the topic.

members.recipe: n<=10: brute force over all n! permutations is fine at a one-second limit. Laaksonen's table pairs n<=10 with O(n!). Past roughly n=12, drop permutations for subset iteration.
members.trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 10?

members.recipe: n<=20: O(2^n) subset enumeration fits a one-second limit. USACO Guide stretches this to O(2^n * n) at n<=20, which is exactly the budget for bitmask DP.
members.trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 20?

members.recipe: n between 25 and 40 with an exponential search: meet in the middle turns 2^n into 2^(n/2). Note 2^(n/2) is sqrt(2^n), a genuinely different complexity class.
members.trigger_condition: Is n too large for 2^n but at most 40?

members.recipe: Quadratic ceiling is contested: Laaksonen says n<=5000 for O(n^2), USACO Guide says n<=7500. Both assume one second. Treat 5000 as safe, 7500 as needing good constants.
members.trigger_condition: Is the input size in the low thousands?

members.recipe: n around 10^5: expect O(n) or O(n log n). Laaksonen notes this directly rules out quadratic, since (10^5)^2 = 10^10 operations takes tens of seconds.
members.trigger_condition: Is the input size about 10^5?

members.recipe: Values up to 10^18: only O(log n), O(log^2 n), or O(1) survive. This signals binary search, binary exponentiation, digit DP, or a closed form rather than enumeration.
members.trigger_condition: Does a bound in the statement exceed 10^9?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which associative container does this access pattern require?
why_exclusive: All four store keys and answer lookups; they are separated by whether order is ever needed, whether rank is ever needed, and whether the key universe is small enough to index directly. Pick the wrong one and the required operation is not merely slow, it is unavailable -- a hash map cannot answer 'predecessor' at all.

members.recipe: Membership tested more than once per element with no ordering needed: hash table, expected amortized O(1) for build, find, insert. Rebuild with a fresh random hash when load factor drifts.
members.trigger_condition: Is membership tested repeatedly without needing key order?

members.recipe: Predecessor, successor, or ordered iteration needed: balanced tree map with worst-case O(log n) insert, lookup, erase. Rust's BTreeMap adds O(log n) range queries that a hash map cannot serve.
members.trigger_condition: Do you need keys near a query key rather than exact?

members.recipe: Need the rank of a key or the k-th smallest element in a dynamic set: g++ policy-based indexed_set supports find_by_order and order_of_key, both logarithmic. Ordinary std::set cannot.
members.trigger_condition: Do you need rank queries on a changing sorted set?

members.recipe: Keys are small integers in a bounded universe u: direct-access array gives worst-case O(1) find, insert, delete. Cost is O(u) space, so this fails once n is far below u.
members.trigger_condition: Do keys fit a small dense integer range?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which Zig allocation strategy fits this lifetime?
why_exclusive: Three answers to one question -- who decides where the memory comes from and when it goes away. They are separated by a single fact each: everything dies at once, the maximum is known when compiling, or the decision is not ours to make. Any two are contradictory advice for the same code.

members.recipe: CLI run, frame loop, or request handler: ArenaAllocator over page_allocator, defer arena.deinit(), free nothing individually. Freeing a non-most-recent allocation inside an arena is a no-op anyway.
members.trigger_condition: Does the code allocate many objects per operation?

members.recipe: Upper bound known at comptime: std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator over a stack buffer, zero heap traffic. Layer it under an arena when the cycle has a known cap.
members.trigger_condition: Is the maximum allocation size known at compile time?

members.recipe: Library code takes an Allocator parameter and lets the caller pick. Do not bake in a global allocator; that decision belongs to the program, not the library.
members.trigger_condition: Is the code a reusable library component?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which TypeScript inference-control tool does this call site need?
why_exclusive: All five keep a literal narrow. They are separated by WHERE the leverage is: on the value, on the callee's signature, on a wrapper because the callee is not ours, on one parameter that must stop voting, or on a check that must not replace the inferred type. Applying the wrong one silently does nothing.

members.recipe: as const does three things: no literal widening, readonly properties, readonly tuples. It applies only to literal expressions — (60*60*1000) as const is an error.
<const T> (5.0) infers as though the caller wrote as const, but only for literals written at the call site. Pass a pre-computed const arr and you still get string[].
When you need literal inference and cannot change the callee, route through a generic identity helper: const asTuple = <const T>(x: T) => x. The type parameter is what makes inference fire.
NoInfer<T> (5.4) stops a position contributing inference candidates. (colors: C[], def?: NoInfer<C>) makes a stray 'blue' an error instead of widening C to include it.
Three different tools: an annotation checks and replaces the type, as asserts without checking, satisfies checks and keeps the inferred type. Reach for satisfies on config objects.

question_the_bucket_answers: Which type-testing tool fits this project's constraints?
why_exclusive: Five tools for one job. The deciding facts are narrow and practical: does a separate command in CI exist, is a dependency acceptable, must several compiler versions be proved at once, and is the assertion about a value or about a line failing to compile.

members.recipe: @ts-expect-error (3.9) suppresses the next line and errors when there was nothing to suppress: 'Unused @ts-expect-error directive'. @ts-ignore is silent either way, so only the former is a test.
type-challenges' assertion pair is Expect<T extends true> and ExpectFalse<T extends false>, used as type cases = [Expect<Equal<Actual, Expected>>]. No runtime, no dependencies.
expectTypeOf(x).toEqualTypeOf<T>() is exact equality, .toExtend<T>() is assignability, .toBeNumber() allows subtypes. Types only — no CLI and no build step.

tsd: expectType<T> is identical-type, expectAssignable/expectNotAssignable are looser, expectError asserts the expression errors, expectNever asserts never, printType prints the computed type. MIT, runs as a CLI.
dtslint's $ExpectType and $ExpectError plus '// Minimum TypeScript Version: x.y' is the DefinitelyTyped convention. The standalone repo is archived; it now ships as @definitelytyped/dtslint.

question_the_bucket_answers: How should this repeated geometry reach the GPU in react-three-fiber?
why_exclusive: Four ways to draw the same thing many times, separated by where the source geometry comes from (written in JSX versus loaded from a file), how many copies there are, whether each copy needs its own React-level behaviour, and whether the bottleneck is submissions or triangles.

members.recipe: <Instances> keeps component ergonomics at one draw call, but each <Instance> carries real CPU overhead. Past a few thousand items, or for foliage, drop to a raw THREE.InstancedMesh. limit sizes the buffer, range the draw range.

When the repeated objects are already-loaded meshes rather than JSX geometry, use <Merged meshes={nodes}>, which yields one component per mesh through a render prop and costs exactly one draw call per type.

<Clone object={nodes.table} /> shallow-clones an Object3D and keeps referencing the original geometries and materials, so reuse is free. deep can be true, 'materialsOnly' or 'geometriesOnly'; inject swaps materials across every mesh inside.

<Detailed distances={[0,10,20]}> wraps THREE.LOD; children go highest quality first and the distance array must match them one to one. Cheapest win when vertex count, not draw calls, is the bottleneck.

question_the_bucket_answers: Which sorting decision does this requirement force?
why_exclusive: All four are about calling a sort, and each is forced by one property of the requirement: ties must not be reordered, the keys are small integers, the sort key is expensive to derive, or only one position in the final order is actually wanted. Two of them cannot both be the answer for one call site.

members.recipe: Need equal elements to keep their input order: use a stable sort. std::sort explicitly does not preserve it; std::stable_sort and Python's sorted do. Java's Object sort is stable, its primitive sort is not.
members.trigger_condition: Must equal-key records retain their original relative order?

members.recipe: Keys are integers in 0..c with c = O(n): counting sort in O(n), escaping the comparison-model lower bound. Only works when the key can index an array directly.
members.trigger_condition: Are sort keys small integers usable as array indices?

members.recipe: Sorting by a derived value: pass a key function, not a comparator. Python's docs note the key is called exactly once per record, while a cmp-style comparator is invoked on every comparison.
members.trigger_condition: Is the sort key expensive to compute per element?

members.recipe: The k-th order statistic once, order of the rest irrelevant: std::nth_element partitions in O(N) average comparisons via introselect, beating a full O(N log N) sort.
members.trigger_condition: Do you need one order statistic without a full ordering?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which allocation fix does this Rust profile call for?
why_exclusive: Four allocation remedies for one language, separated by the SHAPE of the profile: repeated growth of one buffer, one small collection embedded in a hot type, a population that lives and dies together, or a flat cost spread with no hot site. The right one is determined by the profile, not by the topic, and applying another is wasted work.

members.recipe: Vec::with_capacity when the size is known: four allocations collapse to one. Hoist the buffer out of the loop and clear() it. clone_from reuses the destination allocation.
members.trigger_condition: Does the code allocate a Vec of known size repeatedly?

members.recipe: Small collection inside a hot type: SmallVec<[T; N]> stays inline. Mixed borrowed/owned: Cow, not to_string(). format! allocates, so skip it for plain literals.
members.trigger_condition: Does the hot type contain a small fixed-size collection?

members.recipe: Many nodes with one shared lifetime: arena-allocate once, as rustc does with its 'tcx arena, and intern so equality is a pointer compare instead of a deep structural walk.
members.trigger_condition: Do many nodes share one lifetime?

members.recipe: Allocation-heavy workload: try jemalloc or mimalloc before micro-optimizing call sites. Costs binary size and build time, and the win is workload-dependent. Measure it.

question_the_bucket_answers: Which accessibility requirement does this audit finding name?
why_exclusive: Each member is a different subject: indicators, pointer target dimensions, text legibility ratios, programmatic naming, document outline, and vestibular safety. A finding is about one of them and the others are simply not about that finding at all -- exclusivity here comes from topic, not from a condition. This is the control group for the prediction under test.

members.recipe: Keyboard focus must stay visible, themed from your palette, and clear 3:1 against its surroundings. Removing the default outline without replacing it is the commonest regression.
members.trigger_condition: Are you restyling or removing a focus outline?

members.recipe: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels as the Level AA pointer target minimum, with a spacing exception. SC 2.5.5 asks 44 by 44 at AAA.
WCAG AA needs 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text; AAA asks 7:1. Placeholder text is body text for this purpose, not decoration.
Every input needs a programmatic label. A placeholder, an adjacent icon, and an aria-label contradicting the visible text are three distinct failures, not substitutes.
members.trigger_condition: Are you building a form control?

members.recipe: Headings must nest without skipping levels. They are the screen-reader navigation index, not a size picker, so style visual scale separately from semantic level.
members.trigger_condition: Are you choosing a heading tag for its size?

members.recipe: Honour prefers-reduced-motion by removing spatial travel while keeping opacity and state feedback. The vestibular triggers are parallax, large slides, and zoom, not fades.

question_the_bucket_answers: Which finishing failure is this observation?
why_exclusive: Reflow on load, asset weight, unthemed browser chrome, leaked subscriptions and inconsistent iconography are five unrelated subjects. Knowing which one an observation is about requires no comparison between them, which is exactly why this bucket belongs to the topical half.

members.recipe: Set explicit dimensions or aspect-ratio on every image and embed. Unreserved space is layout shift, and layout shift is the most visible craft failure there is.
Do not serve a 3000px asset into a 300px slot. Use srcset with width descriptors, modern formats, and 80-85 percent quality, where the loss is imperceptible.
Theme the surfaces nobody remembers: text selection, caret colour, scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, tabular numerals. Browser defaults are exactly what unfinished looks like.
Clean up listeners, subscriptions, timers, and pending requests on unmount. An interface that gets slower the longer it is used is a craft failure, not a perf one.
members.trigger_condition: Does this component subscribe, poll, or set timers?

members.recipe: Use drawn icons from one coherent set. Emoji and Unicode glyphs as interface icons render differently on every platform and quietly break the visual system.
members.trigger_condition: Are you using emoji or Unicode symbols as icons?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which motion rule does this animation break?
why_exclusive: Animating layout-driving properties, timing bands, easing character, a hint property left switched on, and loops that keep running unseen are five distinct subjects. Any of them could be wrong in the same product at the same time; what makes a bucket member correct here is which one the report is about.

members.recipe: Never animate width, height, top, left, or margins. They drive layout, so every frame costs a reflow and the motion stutters under any load.
100-150ms for immediate feedback, 150-300ms for routine state change, 300-500ms for layout, overlay or view transitions, 500-800ms for one deliberately authored focal entrance.
Do not reach for bounce or elastic easing by reflex. It is the loudest default-AI motion tell and it makes serious interfaces feel like toys.
members.trigger_condition: Did the brief ask for playful or toy-like character?

members.recipe: Apply will-change only during a known animation and remove it afterwards. Left on permanently it costs memory and can make the thing measurably slower.
members.trigger_condition: Are you setting will-change in a stylesheet?

members.recipe: Stop nonessential loops when offscreen or hidden. A looping animation in a background tab is battery drain nobody asked for and nobody sees.
members.trigger_condition: Does any animation loop indefinitely?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which component-behaviour rule does this bug report point at?
why_exclusive: In-flight control state, retaining what the user typed, persistent field naming, distinguishing kinds of emptiness, and rendering very long collections are five separate subjects with no shared condition. One report is about one of them.

members.recipe: Disable the control while its action is in flight. Without it the impatient second click becomes a duplicate charge, message, or record.
members.trigger_condition: Does this control trigger a non-idempotent action?

members.recipe: Preserve user input on error. Clearing a form after a failed submit is the most reliable single way to lose the user entirely.
members.trigger_condition: Can this form fail submission?

members.recipe: Use persistent labels. Placeholders are examples, not labels, and they vanish exactly when the user needs to check what the field wanted.
members.trigger_condition: Are you labelling a form field with a placeholder?

members.recipe: Distinguish first use, no results, filtered-to-nothing, no permission, and failure. One generic nothing-here message collapses five different user situations into one dead end.
members.trigger_condition: Can this list be empty for more than one reason?

members.recipe: Past a few hundred rows, paginate or virtualise. Rendering ten thousand items at once is a design decision that shows up to the user as jank.
members.trigger_condition: Can this list grow past a few hundred items?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which API convention does this review comment invoke?
why_exclusive: Spelling, module and type naming, conversion naming, total-versus-raising pairs, boolean parameters and argument labelling are six independent conventions. They coexist in one style guide and never compete for the same line of code, so choosing between them is a topical identification.

members.recipe: snake_case for values, functions, fields and file names; Capitalized for modules and constructors. Never camelCase. The casing alone tells you what kind of thing you're looking at.
One type, one module, and name the type t. Order.t, not order_t. The module is the namespace, so the type name carries no redundant prefix.
members.trigger_condition: Does the type name repeat its module name?

members.recipe: Conversions are of_ and to_, named for the other type and kept in pairs: Int.of_string, Int.to_string. Not parse, from, as_, convert, or make.
The unsuffixed name is total and returns an option; _exn marks the raising twin. Map.find versus Map.find_exn. The suffix is the warning, visible at the call site.
Kill boolean parameters. f ~force:true says nothing at the call site. A two-constructor variant names both sides and survives the third case you will inevitably add.
members.trigger_condition: Does the existing code contain a boolean parameter?

members.recipe: Label any argument whose type doesn't identify it: ~f, ~init, ~pos, ~len. Two adjacent unlabelled ints are an argument swap waiting to happen.
members.trigger_condition: Are two adjacent arguments both unlabelled integers?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which colour decision does this critique name?
why_exclusive: Authoring space, night-theme derivation, secondary text over a tinted surface, hue count, and where the action colour is spent are five distinct subjects. None of them is a condition on another; a critique is simply about one of them.

members.recipe: If building a new web palette, author it in OKLCH. Lightness and chroma shift predictably there, so ramps stay perceptually even without hand-correcting every step.
members.trigger_condition: Are you defining a new colour palette for web?

members.recipe: Dark mode is a design pass, not an inversion. Re-derive surface elevation and contrast explicitly; a mechanically flipped light theme reads muddy and flat.
members.trigger_condition: Are you adding dark mode to an existing light theme?

members.recipe: Never grey text on a coloured surface. Derive secondary text from that surface hue or its foreground; generic washed grey reads as an unstyled bug.
members.trigger_condition: Is secondary text sitting on a non-neutral coloured surface?

members.recipe: If a surface uses five or more hues, cut to one or two plus neutrals. Colour count is almost never what made the design feel rich.
members.trigger_condition: Does the palette exceed two hues plus neutrals?

members.recipe: Spend the primary action colour on the primary action. If decoration also wears it, the button stops being findable and the hierarchy quietly collapses.
members.trigger_condition: Does decoration share the primary action colour?

question_the_bucket_answers: Which react-three-fiber mechanism explains this behaviour?
why_exclusive: Constructor arguments, nested-property prop syntax, binding a non-scene-graph child to a parent property, automatic teardown of shared assets, and where hooks may be called are five separate mechanisms of the same library. A symptom points at one of them without any comparison between the others.

members.recipe: args is the constructor argument array and only the constructor's. Changing args after mount reconstructs the object from scratch, dropping GPU state and re-running side effects, so never derive args from animated values.

Dash-case pierces into nested properties: rotation-x={1}, shadow-camera-far={50}, material-uniforms-resolution-value={[512,512]}. It saves an object allocation and mutates in place rather than replacing the sub-object.

attach binds a non-Object3D child to a parent property and unbinds on unmount. Anything extending Material or BufferGeometry auto-attaches, so typing attach="material" is redundant. Pierce with attach="attributes-position", index arrays with attach="material-0".

R3F calls .dispose() on every unmounted object it created. If the asset is cached or globally shared, that is a use-after-free: set dispose={null}, which applies to the whole subtree when placed on a parent group.

Every r3f hook reads context, so calling useThree next to <Canvas> rather than inside it crashes. Split the component: the hook belongs in a child rendered by Canvas, not in the component that renders Canvas.

question_the_bucket_answers: Which hidden cost explains this measured surprise?
why_exclusive: An insertion that is linear, a library sort with a conditional fallback, a stack depth limit, a half-implemented union-find, and hash collisions at scale are five unrelated causes. They cannot both explain one measurement, but telling them apart is recognising the subject, not weighing a condition.

members.recipe: bisect.insort is O(n), not O(log n): the Python docs state the logarithmic search is dominated by the linear insertion step. Finding the position is cheap; making room is not.
members.trigger_condition: Are you inserting into an array-backed sorted list repeatedly?

members.recipe: std::stable_sort is O(N log N) only when its temporary buffer allocation succeeds. If allocation fails it silently falls back to O(N log^2 N). Memory pressure is a complexity risk.
members.trigger_condition: Is memory tight while sorting a very large range?

members.recipe: Recursion depth is a hard resource, not an asymptotic one. Python's limit exists to stop C stack overflow crashing the interpreter; the highest safe value is platform-dependent and raising it can crash.
members.trigger_condition: Can recursion depth grow linearly with the input size?

members.recipe: DSU with only path compression is O(log n) per query; with only union by rank it is also O(log n). The near-constant inverse Ackermann bound requires both optimisations together.
members.trigger_condition: Did you implement only one of the two DSU optimisations?

members.recipe: Birthday paradox on hashes: one comparison collides with probability 1/m, but 10^6 mutual comparisons against m = 10^9+9 makes a collision near certain. Use two moduli to reach an effective 10^18.
members.trigger_condition: Are you comparing far more than sqrt(modulus) hashed items?
